title: The Doctor China Remembered
shortDescription: A doctor from a middle-class family in Solapur who sailed to China in 1938 with a five-man medical mission, operated for the Communist Eighth Route Army, married a Chinese nurse and died at thirty-two. China built him memorials, printed his face on stamps and still brings leaders to his family's door. In India, his own country, he is almost unknown.
introduction: Sholapur, 1938. A young doctor asked his family's permission to go to China. They gave it. He never came home. Four years later he died in northern China at thirty-two, and two countries made different memories of him. In China they carved his name into stone and printed it on stamps. In India, the country that sent him, his name barely registers. This is the story of Dwarkanath Shantaram Kotnis, who crossed the sea to serve in a war that was not his own, and became one man held in two very different memories.

chapters.heading: Sholapur
paragraphs: Nobody in the Kotnis household knew much about China. They knew it because men came to the door selling Chinese silk. That was how his sister Manorama remembered it years later, and the detail tells you what lay ahead. Dwarkanath Shantaram Kotnis was born in Sholapur on 10 October 1910 into a middle-class Maharashtrian family. His father worked in the city's textile mills and held a position in the municipality. It was a known family in a known town — not poor, not grand. The boy grew up with a taste for travel that the town could not quite hold.

Solapur had known plague. During one outbreak the family moved out of the city, and the memory stayed with him. He entered medical college intending to become a surgeon. But the colleges of Bombay in the 1930s were political places. He enrolled at Seth G. S. Medical College, founded in 1926 by Indian nationalists as an answer to the British-run Grant Medical College, and was swept into a student strike there. The authorities told him to leave and continue his studies at Grant. He went. In 2011 researchers found his old career card at Grant — a small rectangle of paper recording internships in vaccination and in winter and summer infections. That card is the quiet physical trace of the years that made him a doctor. He qualified with an MBBS in 1936.

His family wanted him to marry, settle in Sholapur and practise near home. It was a reasonable wish, and a safe one. He wanted surgery. He wanted to travel. The wish to go somewhere took hold of him, and he asked permission before accepting the posting to China. His family agreed. He was twenty-seven, unmarried, and about to board a ship. He would learn the language of the country those silk sellers came from. He would spend the rest of his life there. He never saw Sholapur again.

media.alt: A black-and-white portrait of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis photographed in China in the 1940s
media.caption: Kotnis in China in the 1940s, in a photograph preserved in Chinese archives and now held on Wikimedia Commons under a public-domain licence.

chapters.heading: The call
paragraphs: The request came from a general on the other side of the world. Zhu De, commander of the Chinese Communist forces fighting Japan, wrote to Jawaharlal Nehru asking for doctors. Nehru carried it to the Indian National Congress, and Congress formed a committee to raise money and choose a team. More than seven hundred people volunteered; about a hundred of them were doctors. The committee picked five.

Subhas Chandra Bose, as Congress president, had already set the machinery in motion. On 30 June 1938 he issued a press statement declaring an All-India China Day on 12 June, fixing fund-raising days for 7 to 9 July, and announcing that an ambulance had been ordered from Ford's, to be sent straight to Hong Kong. The Congress's fifty-second session passed the resolution. One doctor, Ranen Sen, was selected first but refused permission by the British because he was a communist. He suggested Bejoy Kumar Basu in his place. That is how the team came together — through a committee, a rejection and a substitute. The five were Madan Mohan Lal Atal of Allahabad, a veteran of medical aid in the Spanish Civil War, who led them; M. R. Cholkar of Nagpur; Basu and Debesh Mukherjee of Calcutta; and Kotnis from Sholapur.

On 31 August 1938 a public meeting at Jinnah Hall in Bombay said goodbye to them. Sarojini Naidu, the poet and independence leader who chaired it, fastened Red Cross bands onto their arms. She warned them that some, or one of them, might not come back. It was the sort of sentence people remember afterwards, when they know which one it was.

The next morning they sailed from Ballard Pier on the SS Rajputana. Basu's diary remembered Kotnis so heavily garlanded that nothing showed except his weary, exultant face. The ship called at Colombo, Penang, Singapore and Hong Kong. They reached Guangzhou on 17 September. At a banquet there, Soong Ching-ling, the widow of Sun Yat-sen, watched the Indian doctors fumble with their chopsticks. She dipped her own hand into the chicken. 'God has given fingers to pick up food,' she said. It was a small kindness, and the young men were a long way from home.

chapters.heading: Yan'an
paragraphs: Yan'an was a cave-city cut into the hills of Shaanxi — party offices, schools and hospitals carved into the earth, from which the Eighth Route Army directed the war behind Japanese lines. Kotnis arrived in February 1939, aged twenty-eight. To a doctor who had known only silk merchants, it was another planet. He met Mao Zedong the following month. In July he treated Zhou Enlai, later China's premier, after a fall from a horse. Such moments fill the official accounts. The truer measure of his life there is quieter: he learned the language, took a Chinese name, Ke Dihua, and stayed.

That name is carved on the memorials and written in the hospital registers. The English one appears on an Indian stamp. He was one of very few foreigners inside the Communist base area, and movement in and out of it grew harder as the war settled into its long middle years.

In November 1939 he left Yan'an for Wuxiang, headquarters of the Eighth Route Army, and then for Jin-Cha-Ji, the border region where Shanxi, Chahar and Hebei meet. This was guerrilla country — villages, mountain tracks, field hospitals that folded up and moved when the army moved. Surgery there meant wounds, infection and amputations with whatever instruments could be carried. He operated. He taught. He began writing surgical textbooks in Chinese because the students he trained had almost nothing to learn from.

Of the five who had sailed together, some went home. Cholkar returned in May 1939; Mukherjee left the same year after falling ill. Nehru wrote in April 1939 that the mission was expected to remain at least another year, and that Atal and Basu had offered to stay as long as the Chinese wanted them. Kotnis was not named in that appeal. He stayed the longest. The mission had been planned as a year's service. It became the rest of his life.

chapters.heading: The hospital in the mountains
paragraphs: Norman Bethune was already a legend in the base areas when Kotnis reached them. The Canadian surgeon had come to China in 1938, established medical services for the Communist forces and trained doctors and nurses in the mountain hospitals. He died on 12 November 1939 of blood poisoning contracted during an operation. Kotnis laid a wreath at his tomb. Chinese commemorations cast him as Bethune's successor, and in 1941 he became director of the Bethune International Peace Hospital in Shijiazhuang. He taught at the Bethune Hygiene School of the Jin-Cha-Ji Military Command. The hospital and the school carried the Canadian's name; the Indian doctor inherited both. The school trained medical workers for the Eighth Route Army, and he taught there while running the hospital.

He worked in a hospital named for a man he had never operated alongside. He operated on wounds and infections in field hospitals that moved with the army, taught nurses and doctors in a language he had had to learn as an adult, and compiled surgical manuals in Chinese so that the students he trained could learn from them after he was gone. There is a particular kind of care in writing a textbook for people you will not be there to help. That is what he was doing.

One letter from this period survives. He wrote it in April 1942 to Bejoy Kumar Basu, the Calcutta doctor who had sailed with him and stayed. It sits in a collection of more than seventy of his letters. In it he tells Basu that he regards 1941 as one of the most important years of his life. He does not say why in the passage that is usually quoted. A man does not write that about a year he has merely endured.

media.alt: An old black-and-white photograph of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis laying a wreath at a memorial to Dr. Norman Bethune
media.caption: Kotnis laying a wreath in memory of Norman Bethune, the Canadian surgeon whose work with the Eighth Route Army he continued. In 1941 he became director of the hospital that bears Bethune's name.
media.credit: Unknown photographer, reproduced on Wikimedia Commons — Public domain (China)

chapters.heading: Yinhua
paragraphs: In 1941, at the Bethune International Peace Hospital in Shijiazhuang, Kotnis married Guo Qinglan. She was a Chinese nurse working at the hospital. The building had been named for a Canadian surgeon who had died two years earlier, so the wedding took place inside a monument to another foreign doctor. She was known in later life as Guo Qinglan Kotnis. Chinese leaders visiting India would ask after her, decades after he was gone.

Their son was born on 23 August 1942. Nie Rongzhen, a senior Communist commander, suggested the name. They called him Yinhua: yin is the short form of Yin-du, India; hua is China. Chinese-language records give the full name as Ke Yinhua, using the surname his father had taken. The boy was born in the hospital where his father worked, in the middle of a war. Two countries, two characters, one child. It was the only name they ever gave a child, and it held both of them inside it. It is the most precise thing anyone ever said about this life, and it needs no speech to explain it.

The child was not yet four months old when his father died. He grew up in China and died there in 1967, twenty-five years after him. Guo Qinglan outlived her husband by sixty-nine years. She died in Dalian in 2011 at the age of ninety-six. She had remarried, but she kept the name Guo Qinglan Kotnis. For the rest of her life she appeared in the records of her own country as the widow of an Indian doctor who had died in a war between China and Japan. Sixty-nine years is a long time to keep a name. That is what it meant.

chapters.heading: The last page
paragraphs: Kotnis had epilepsy. He kept the condition to himself, and the strain of the work made it worse. He carried on operating, teaching and writing until his body gave way. Chinese state media record that on 8 December 1942 he collapsed while writing a second surgery textbook for his Chinese students. He died the next day, 9 December, at thirty-two. He never saw the film that would be made about him four years later. He had sailed to China as a young man who wanted surgery and travel. He died a teacher who had written the books his students would learn from. A surgeon who had spent four years teaching others died over the book he meant them to use.

His remains were laid in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang, among the martyrs of the wars China fought in the twentieth century. He was one of the few foreigners buried there. His Chinese wife and his infant son were in the country he had made his home.

There is a temptation to end such a life with triumph. The facts resist it. He was a young doctor who answered a letter, crossed an ocean, learned a language, worked until he broke, and left behind a wife, a child and a grave. The 1946 Indian film about him, Dr. Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani, directed by V. Shantaram and written by K. A. Abbas and V. P. Sathe from Abbas's And One Did Not Come Back, gave him a grander ending. The real one is quieter and, in its way, harder to bear.

media.alt: The tomb of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang, Hebei province
media.caption: His Chinese-style tomb in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery at Shijiazhuang. His remains were brought here after his death in 1942.

chapters.heading: A hero in two countries
paragraphs: The film made him a household name in India for a time. Dr. Kotnis Ki Amar Kahani was released in 1946, directed by V. Shantaram, written by K. A. Abbas and V. P. Sathe from Abbas's And One Did Not Come Back. China made its own film, Ke Di Hua Dai Fu, in 1982. China issued stamps in 1982 and 1992; India issued one on 9 December 1993, fifty-one years after his death. In 2009 a Chinese internet poll named him among the ten foreign friends who had done most for China in a century. Chinese leaders have called on his family in India for decades — a ritual of a friendship that predates the border war of 1962.

The memorials are easier to count than the memory. There is one in Shijiazhuang and a memorial hall in Tang County, where he worked and died. A hall at the Bethune International Peace Hospital carries his name, and so does the Kotnis India-China Friendship Hospital at Hebei Medical University. In Solapur, his birthplace, a memorial hospital opened in 1976 and his former residence became a memorial in 2012. New exhibition halls opened in Hebei in December 2025. Official Chinese media call him Dr Thoughtful and Old Ke — names of affection, not ceremony.

'At home, Dr Kotnis appears to be a little-known figure these days. In China he is revered as a hero.' The BBC wrote that in 2013. The Indian historian Vinay Lal put it more sharply: adulation, even veneration, in China; largely forgotten in India. The generation that saw the 1946 film has passed. The other four doctors of the mission have faded too. The 1962 war changed how each country told the story. What remains is a name on a hospital in Hebei, a name on a street in Solapur, a stamp in an album, and a son's two-character name.

media.alt: A memorial statue of Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis at the North China Martyrs' Cemetery in Shijiazhuang
media.caption: The memorial statue at Shijiazhuang, where his remains were laid in the North China Martyrs' Cemetery after his death in 1942.

chapters.heading: What remains
paragraphs: The record of this life survives in ordinary things. There is Nehru's appeal for the mission, with its request that donations be sent to Congress House in Bombay. There is Basu's diary of the voyage, with the garlands and the chopsticks. There is the career card found at Grant Medical College in 2011, a rectangle of paper naming two kinds of infection. There are more than seventy letters preserved in a Chinese collection. There are two countries' postage stamps, a film catalogue entry at the British Film Institute, and a grave in Shijiazhuang. None of these is a monument. Together they are a life.

He sailed from Bombay in September 1938 at twenty-seven and never came back. He learned the language of the country he had known through silk sellers. He worked in hospitals that moved with an army, taught students from books he wrote himself, married one of their nurses and gave his son a name made of two countries. He died at thirty-two, was buried among China's martyrs, and was printed on an Indian stamp fifty-one years later. China kept him because he served its people in their worst year. India let him go.

The photograph on this page came back from China. That is where his memory survived, and that is where a reader has to go to find him. In Solapur the memorial hospital has stood since 1976, and his former residence became a memorial in 2012. In Hebei, where he spent his last years, a memorial hall stands in Tang County and new halls opened in December 2025. The films, Indian in 1946 and Chinese in 1982, remain the screen records of his life. Two countries, one doctor, and a name neither has quite let go.

media.alt: The 1993 Indian postage stamp commemorating Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis, showing his portrait
media.caption: India Post issued this stamp on 9 December 1993, fifty-one years after his death. It is the clearest sign that the country which sent him had begun to remember him too.
media.credit: India Post, Government of India — GODL-India

sources.title: 'An Indian doctor in China', Mumbai Mirror opinion column by Sanjay Nagral
sources.note: By surgeon-historian Sanjay Nagral. Supports the plague outbreak that led the family to leave Sholapur, his admission to Seth G. S. Medical College and his move to Grant after a student strike, his 1936 qualification, and his family's wish that he settle in Sholapur.

sources.title: 'Dr. Dwarkanath Kotnis' feature and biography

sources.note: Indian government account. Supports the 10 October 1910 birth, the middle-class family, the five mission doctors, his wish to travel and practise surgery, his family's permission, his sister Manorama's recollection of the silk sellers, the 1946 film and the 1993 Indian stamp.

sources.title: 'Why is India's Dr Kotnis revered in China?'
sources.note: Supports the marriage to Guo Qinglan, the 2009 Chinese internet poll, Chinese leaders visiting his family, and the contrast between his status in China and his obscurity in India, quoted directly in the story.

sources.title: 'Framing discourse on China in the modern world'

sources.note: Academic account by Vinay Lal. Supports the reading of Kotnis as a figure of pre-1962 India-China solidarity and the contrast between veneration in China and being forgotten in India.

sources.title: 'The undying influence and memory of Dr Kotnis'
sources.note: Indian think-tank reconstruction. Supports the itinerary — Yan'an in February 1939, the meeting with Mao in March, treating Zhou Enlai in July, Wuxiang and Jin-Cha-Ji — and the naming of his son Yinhua.

sources.title: 'Doctor's inspiring legacy given a fresh take'
sources.note: Chinese state media, used only for the commemorative record. Supports his 1941 directorship of the Bethune International Peace Hospital, his work with the Eighth Route Army, and his collapse on 8 December 1942 while writing a second surgery textbook.

sources.title: 'Wife of Dwarkanath Kotnis is no more'
sources.note: Supports Guo Qinglan's death in Dalian in 2011 at the age of ninety-six, her retained married name, and Kotnis's epilepsy.

sources.note: Reproduces Bose's 30 June 1938 press statement in full: All-India China Day on 12 June, fund days on 7–9 July, the ordered ambulance and the Congress mechanism. Also documents Ranen Sen's selection and his substitution of Basu.

sources.title: 'Remembering Dr Kotnis', by M. Bapuji
